blocks.text: Entrepreneurship
Cycle 1: From a Medical Device to an Agricultural Screening Platform
DESIGN. The SynBioBeta poster listed medical point-of-care testing next to agriculture; more applications seemed more valuable.
BUILD. SynBioBeta 2026 (San Jose, May 4–7): Next-Gen BioLeader and Expo Hall poster, reporting target metrics only.

TEST. Investors and founders asked whether living cells can scale, how a medical device would be regulated, and whether the hardware has enough margin. A UCLA PhD student had not understood how a live-cell sensor is built.
LEARN. A long application list hides very different paths to market; a diagnostic device faces a far heavier approval path.
REDESIGN. First application moved from medical to agriculture; medical kept as a long-term lead. The scale question is still open.
Cycle 2: From Six Crops to One Beachhead
DESIGN. A general "facility agriculture disease detection" platform across six crops, sized against the e-nose instrument market (US$164M in 2026 to US$293M by 2031).
BUILD. Full business plan submitted to FITI, the national startup program.

TEST. June open call, July mentor session, and August 11-point review all asked who pays and why spread so thin. Core objection: find the market's pain first, then check your strength addresses it. Our sizing never connected to a customer's loss.
LEARN. What a technology can do is not a customer with one expensive problem.
REDESIGN. One beachhead: banana disease detection in Taiwan's export chain, with mango and tea as follow-ons. Sizing rebuilt bottom-up: TAM ≈ NT$113.6B, SAM ≈ NT$15–18B, SOM ≈ NT$20M per year.
Cycle 3: From "An E-Nose That Does Many Things" to a Positioned Platform
DESIGN. Showing the platform's versatility would persuade reviewers.
BUILD. 13-page deck, technology-first, comparing us with Alpha MOS, Aryballe, and Sensigent mainly on analysis cycle time.

TEST. Slide-level review: it reads as "an e-nose that can do a lot of things," not a customer with an expensive problem. Cycle time is where lab instruments beat us, and the team slide never said why we can build this.
LEARN. Lead with who it is for. The wrong comparison axis turns a differentiator into a weakness.

REDESIGN. Repositioned as a B2B Agricultural VOC Intelligence Platform (banana and mango near-term, tea Phase 2). Seven-axis matrix without cycle time, four revenue layers, capability-matrix team slide. The 18-page deck marks unconfirmed numbers as pending.
Cycle 4: From "Cheaper Than a Lab Instrument" to "The Lab's Screening Layer"
DESIGN. Part of our value was being a cheaper alternative to GC-MS and LC-MS.
BUILD. Interview with an analytical-instrumentation professional with GC-MS/LC-MS testing-service experience.

TEST. By the interviewee's own figures (unverified), an instrument costs about NT$5–10M over ~15 years plus NT$200–300k per year to maintain: not the real barrier. Trained staff and lab infrastructure are. Telling closely related microbes apart matters more than flagging an off odor. Individual farmers have low willingness to pay; buyers are associations, improvement stations, cooperatives, and certifiers.
LEARN. "Cheaper than the lab" was the wrong axis.

REDESIGN. Fast · On-site · Low operator dependence: a screening layer that sends flagged samples to the lab. Buyer segment corrected. Semiconductor, humanitarian-shipping, and authenticity leads logged as unvalidated and kept out of the banana beachhead.
Cycle 5: From "The Smell Is in the Fruit" to "The Smell Is at the Base of the Plant"
DESIGN. Our beachhead assumed the diseases we can smell are in the fruit by the time it reaches the packing house.
BUILD. September 25 interview with a pest-and-disease specialist at the Taiwan Banana Research Institute (Pingtung), using the institute's growth-stage guide.

TEST. Expert judgment, not measurement. Strongest odors come from the corm, pseudostem, and crown (weevils, soft rot, crown rot, Fusarium wilt); fruit-side problems are faint. Fusarium wilt is obvious only late; an early signal exists but is faint, with no day count. A dirty orchard also smells strong. An institute is likelier to pay than a farmer. His question: can it really measure accurately?
LEARN. Where we look was set by our reasoning, only partly supported. Institutions as buyers is now confirmed by a second source. We make no detection-window claim.

REDESIGN (proposed). Field rot detection added as candidate targets, scored with the Detectability × Consequence × Unmet Need × Willingness to Pay framework. Institute proposed as a pilot site (no agreement). Sampling gets an orchard-hygiene control.
Cycle 6: From "It Detects a Smell" to "It Works in the Field, and We Can Protect It"
DESIGN. Five cycles described a bench sensor. Field use and IP were untested.
BUILD. A researcher at the Taoyuan District Agricultural Improvement Station (Plant Protection Lab); local farmers' associations; a patent attorney.

TEST. Station: no monitoring exists beyond looking at the crop, so no data are collected. The researcher asked which disease, how many sampling points per plot, and what the returned data mean; a remote-vehicle idea was possible in theory but impractical. Associations: confirmed real sampling and post-harvest handling, which fed our loss framing. Attorney: a claim needs novelty, an inventive step, and industrial applicability. A receptor mutation suits an invention patent; the whole system may suit a utility model (form examination only, 10 years against 20). Our own disclosures can become prior art: Taiwan gives a one-year grace period, China and Europe are stricter, and it does not stop others filing first. A US provisional secures an early date; the university is normally the applicant.
LEARN. "Detects a smell" is not "works in a field," and we have no field data to answer the station's questions. Our IP position is undefined: no prior-art search, nothing filed.
REDESIGN. The station's questions become acceptance criteria for a first field trial. IP steps: university route to a possible US provisional, prior-art search, choose target countries.
Education
Cycle 1: From "The Public Doesn't Understand Mold" to the Risks People Cannot See
DESIGN. The public broadly misunderstands mold, so education should correct that gap.
BUILD. Bilingual online survey, 300 respondents; its misconception items served as a diagnostic pre-test.

TEST. Understanding fell as risk became less visible: 78% (removing visible mold is not enough), 64% (heat does not destroy all mycotoxins), 58% (normal look and smell is not safe), with about 15% holding the misconception on the last. Higher-knowledge respondents (n = 180) recorded the opening date more often than the rest (n = 120): 42% vs 25%. Even so, 58% of them did not. Top needs from a screening tool: trustworthy results 76%, avoiding missed risk 73%, clear next steps 68%.
LEARN. The gap is a decision habit about invisible risks, not missing facts, so a lecture is the wrong tool. The sample is self-selected: it shows where to look, not how common a belief is.
REDESIGN. Two target claims: heat does not detoxify mycotoxins and look and smell are not a safety check. Format changed from talk to decision-based game.
Cycle 2: From a Diagnosed Misconception to a Playable Intervention
DESIGN. Making a choice and seeing its cost lands closer to the two claims than being told, and works for adults and children.

BUILD. Odor Pixel Suite: Pattern Recognition, Odor Maze, and Odor Fingerprint Mixer (8–25 minutes each). Educator mode gives a paired pre/post test and anonymous export. Colorblind-safe palette, alt text, and icon plus label on every risk color.

TEST. Qualitative only. At the camp, the game ran as a whole-class activity: of 22 worksheets, 5 mentioned the game, and pupils called it "really hard" and said it had "a lot of questions." At the workshop, 15 students tried it.
LEARN. Children could take part once the game became whole-class (teams answer by finger count). Complaints were difficulty and length, not the idea. Correction of the two claims is untested.
REDESIGN. Released as an open resource, with the pre/post question set documented for reuse.
Cycle 3: From One Game to a Five-Module Curriculum
DESIGN. One game does not cover the whole chain from biology to a screening decision.

BUILD. AeroSense Learning Lab: five modules of about 8 minutes (Discover, Question, Build, Decode, Decide), three check questions each. The Question items repeat the survey statements word for word, so survey, game, and curriculum form one measurement chain.
TEST / LEARN. More than 500 people have gone through it.
REDESIGN. Platform-level changes: text cut, color blocks added, easier opening and closing, hands-on tasks.
Cycle 4: From a Website to Real Audiences, and Outside Validation
DESIGN. Websites reach only people who seek them out; we needed live audiences with a recorded baseline, and expert scrutiny.

BUILD. Reach: Instagram series, sustainability pop quiz, short videos, articles on Prof. Lo's lab blog. Camp, Oct 12: 30+ grade 5 pupils at a rural school in Xinfeng, Hsinchu County (mini-class, whole-class game, drawing). Workshop, Oct 14, with Prof. Lo for NTHU life-science and medical students (QR pre-test, two talks, platform and games, feedback form). Outside: China Medical University lecture (Sept 23) and the Mini Jamboree hosted by iGEM TAU-Israel (Oct 8; 8 teams, 6 countries).

TEST. Reach: feed posts reached 1,700+ accounts, stories 1,400+, reels 500+; this shows interest, not learning. Camp: of 22 worksheets, 13 named something learned and 9 wrote only that they had fun. Workshop: 15 students (about five each doctoral, master's, bachelor's); Prof. Lo's talk rated highest and participants strongly agreed they understood better (self-reported). Comments: English terms were hard, they wanted a take-home message, and they wanted the neural network, goal, and intended use explained more clearly. Lecture: 30+ students, mostly asking how sensor readings become a decision.
LEARN. Two audiences asked for the same thing: a plainer account of how the model reads a smell. Four in ten pupils wrote only that they had fun, which is engagement, not understanding.

REDESIGN. Model introduction made plainer after the lecture, and the workshop showed it was not enough: a take-home overview and clearer neural-network explanation come next. The school principal asked to keep using the approach, so we packaged a free Teacher Toolkit (slides, game, Learning Lab instructions); the school's Director of Student Affairs said it lets children "access science knowledge in a correct and fun way." The Education Guide gives other teams the steps.
